title: IT Act s. 66 — Computer related offences (Hacking) (IT Act s. 66)

content.overview: Computer related offences under IT Act section 66: acts referred to in section 43 become punishable when done dishonestly or fraudulently, subject to the statutory requirements.
content.glance: Computer related offences under IT Act section 66: acts referred to in section 43 become punishable when done dishonestly or fraudulently, subject to the statutory requirements.
content.study: Section 66 is the criminalisation layer for specified section 43 conduct when the statutory dishonest or fraudulent mental element is established. Analyse the underlying section 43 act first, then prove dishonesty or fraud, attribution and the digital record. Electronic records should be assessed under BSA 2023 section 63 where applicable, separately from attribution and merits. Distinguish section 66 from civil compensation under section 43 and from other IT Act offences.

sections.heading: Evidence and attribution
sections.body: Map logs, device records, credentials and communications to the accused and the underlying section 43 act; apply BSA section 63 where applicable.

sections.heading: Boundaries
sections.body: Separate compensation under section 43 from criminal liability under section 66 and from other offences whose ingredients differ.

sections.heading: Defence and consequence
sections.body: Test authority, consent, attribution, mental element and evidentiary gaps before stating the criminal consequence.

cases.name: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India
cases.facts: The Court reviewed restrictions on online speech under the Information Technology Act.
cases.issue: Whether IT Act s. 66A impermissibly restricted constitutional speech.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Section 66A was vague and overbroad and violated Article 19(1)(a); it was not saved by Article 19(2).
cases.holding: Section 66A was struck down in its entirety.
cases.relevance: Use only as historical status; do not present s. 66A as a current offence.

cases.name: Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer
cases.facts: The Court examined the statutory method for proving electronic records.
cases.issue: Whether electronic records can be admitted without the applicable certificate route.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Electronic records must satisfy the special statutory proof requirements applicable to computer outputs.
cases.holding: The Court reaffirmed the certificate discipline for electronic evidence.
cases.relevance: Use with BSA s. 63 and digital-record admissibility.

cases.name: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
cases.facts: The Constitution Bench considered privacy as a constitutional right in the digital and modern State.
cases.issue: Whether privacy is protected as a Fundamental Right.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Privacy is intrinsic to dignity, liberty and Part III, subject to legality, legitimate aim, proportionality and procedural safeguards.
cases.relevance: Use for surveillance, data protection and informational privacy.
